title: India’s 2,100 Global Capability Centers Now Employ 2.36 Million, Reshaping Cities and Careers Across the Country
excerpt: From cost-saving back offices to strategic innovation hubs, GCCs are transforming India’s employment landscape and commercial real estate market as states compete to attract the next wave of centers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's 2,100 Global Capability Centers employ 2.36 million professionals, generating nearly $100 billion annually.
  • GCCs have transformed from back offices to innovation hubs focusing on AI and advanced analytics.
  • States are competing for GCCs, with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh introducing attractive policies and incentives.
  • India's commercial real estate market is projected to exceed 1 billion square feet of office space by 2030.

  • India now hosts over 2,100 Global Capability Centers employing nearly 2.36 million professionals and generating close to $100 billion in annual revenue.
  • GCCs have evolved from cost-saving back offices into strategic innovation hubs handling research, product development, AI, and advanced analytics for global corporations.
  • States including Bihar, Kerala, Maharashtra, and Uttar Pradesh are competing aggressively with new GCC policies and incentives to attract centers beyond Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
  • The commercial real estate market is being reshaped, with India projected to have more than 1 billion square feet of premium office space by 2030.

The Scale of India’s GCC Ecosystem

India’s Global Capability Centers have grown into one of the most significant pillars of the country’s services economy. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, which launched its Global Orbit Summit 2026 series this month, reported that the country now hosts over 2,100 GCCs employing nearly 2.36 million professionals and generating close to $100 billion in annual revenue.

The centers, which serve as offshore operational arms of multinational corporations, have undergone a fundamental transformation over the past decade. What began as cost-arbitrage operations handling basic IT support and back-office processing have evolved into strategic hubs performing research, product development, advanced analytics, and increasingly, artificial intelligence work.

A report by Taggd in partnership with the Confederation of Indian Industry and JLL India found that 48 percent of GCCs planned to increase hiring in fiscal year 2026, with early-career lateral talent possessing one to five years of experience remaining the core hiring focus.

The Race Beyond Metro Cities

The most significant shift in India’s GCC landscape is the push into tier-2 and tier-3 cities. While Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR, and Hyderabad remain the dominant hubs — 60 percent of GCCs still hire exclusively from these six established centers — 29 percent now plan to hire across a mix of tier-1 and tier-2 cities, and 13 percent expect to recruit in tier-2 and tier-3 locations.

State governments are competing intensely for this investment. Bihar introduced its GCC Policy 2026, offering incentives linked to fixed capital investment, rentals, and employment, with additional benefits for companies hiring local domiciles. Uttar Pradesh is positioning Lucknow and other cities as attractive alternatives, citing strong policy support, modern infrastructure, and a large pool of STEM graduates.

“GCCs are now likely to move to tier-two, tier-three cities to actually capitalize on the competitive edge these cities provide.”

— Kundan Kumar, Secretary, Department of Industries, Government of Bihar

Maharashtra is expanding its focus beyond Mumbai and Pune, promoting Nagpur, Nashik, and Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar as future GCC destinations with stamp duty subsidies and digital ease-of-doing-business initiatives. Kerala is positioning itself through an AI-focused industrial strategy, pitching the state as “a rural urban continuum where quality of life is assured across tier-2 and tier-3 cities.”

Reshaping Commercial Real Estate

The GCC expansion is driving significant changes in India’s commercial real estate market. A Colliers report projected that India will have more than 1 billion square feet of premium office space by 2030, driven largely by GCC demand. The main metropolitan areas of Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR, and Hyderabad are expected to see declining vacancy rates as demand absorbs available supply, with gradual rental price increases in prime business districts.

Companies are increasingly prioritizing green-certified premium buildings, and the growing flexible workspace segment is reshaping how GCCs approach real estate. The shift reflects a broader trend toward employee-centric workspace design and distributed workforce strategies.

Challenges Ahead

The US HIRE Act 2025, introduced in the Senate, poses a potential threat to the GCC model. The bill proposes a 25 percent excise tax on payments made by US firms to foreign service providers, which could significantly raise the cost of maintaining offshore operations. The Global Trade Research Initiative warned that even in-house GCCs of US multinationals operating in India may not be insulated, as the tax applies to any payment benefiting US consumers.

Indian technology firms may face pressure to expand local US staffing, accept lower margins, or accelerate their shift toward higher-value digital, AI, cybersecurity, and consulting services. Gen Z workforce trends add another dimension — average tenure expectations have decreased significantly, with young professionals preferring not to remain in the same role for more than 18 to 24 months.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRI professionals, the GCC boom creates compelling return-to-India career opportunities in global roles at competitive compensation. The expansion into tier-2 cities also opens options beyond the high-cost metros, while the centers’ focus on AI, cloud, and cybersecurity mirrors the skill sets many diaspora professionals have built in Silicon Valley and other US tech hubs.
